item.title: Sorakuen Garden: Kobe's Finest Traditional Garden — Guide
item.description: Sorakuen is the finest traditional Japanese garden in Kobe, laid out in the Meiji era as the private grounds of a former city mayor and opened to the public after the war. Its winding paths circle a pond fed by a waterfall, passing through groves of pine, camphor and maple in the middle of the modern city. Two unusual buildings share the grounds: the Hassam House, a Western-style villa built for a British trader in Kobe’s foreign settlement, and a rare surviving feudal-lord’s stable relocated here — and each May the garden’s several thousand azaleas turn it brilliant.

item.title: Isuien and Yoshikien: Nara Park's Strolling Gardens — Guide
item.description: Tucked beside the bustle of Nara Park near Todaiji lie two of the city’s loveliest Japanese gardens. Isuien is a classic strolling garden built around ponds and teahouses, celebrated for its masterful use of shakkei, ‘borrowed scenery’, framing the distant Todaiji Nandaimon gate and the green hills of Mount Wakakusa within its own composition — different in every season and paired with the fine Neiraku Museum of ancient art. Next door, Yoshikien offers three distinct gardens — a pond garden, a moss garden and a tea-ceremony garden — in a compact, tranquil space that most visitors miss.

item.title: Kenrokuen Garden: One of Japan's Three Great Gardens — Guide
item.description: Kenrokuen Garden is ranked among Japan’s three most celebrated landscape gardens, its name meaning ‘garden of six attributes’, referring to the qualities of spaciousness, seclusion, artifice, antiquity, water and panoramic views that traditional garden theory considered essential to a perfect garden. Developed by the Maeda clan over roughly two centuries, the garden combines ponds, streams, teahouses and trees several hundred years old, and each winter its pine trees are fitted with distinctive rope supports called yukitsuri to protect their branches from heavy snowfall, creating a striking seasonal sight.

item.title: Fujita Memorial Garden: Hirosaki's Taisho Garden — Guide
item.description: The Fujita Memorial Garden in Hirosaki is a refined two-level garden from the Taisho era. An upper garden with a Western villa and a lower garden with a pond and waterfall frame distant views of Mt. Iwaki — a peaceful stop away from the castle crowds. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hirosaki, Aomori Hours ~9:00–17:00 (seasonal) Admission Around ¥320 Time needed About 1 hour Best time Spring–autumn; fresh green & foliage What to See The elegant upper garden with a Taisho-era Western villa.

item.title: Isuien & Yoshikien Gardens: Nara's Best Gardens — Guide
item.description: Just north of Nara Park sit two of the city’s loveliest strolling gardens. Isuien is a refined pond garden that ‘borrows’ the scenery of Todai-ji’s gate and the eastern hills, while neighbouring Yoshikien offers three gardens — pond, moss and tea-flower — and is free to foreign visitors. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Suimoncho, Nara (near Todai-ji) Hours 9:30–16:30 (Isuien closed Tue); Yoshikien ~9:00–17:00 Admission Isuien ¥1,200; Yoshikien free for foreign visitors Time needed 1 hour for both Best time Fresh green (May) & autumn maples What to See Isuien — a two-part pond garden framing Todai-ji’s Nandaimon and Mt.

item.title: Hamarikyu Gardens Guide: A Tidal Garden Between the Skyscrapers
item.description: Few places capture the strange beauty of Tokyo like Hamarikyu. Step inside the walls of this 300-year-old feudal garden and you’re surrounded by pine forests, a tidal seawater pond, and a teahouse on an island reached by wooden bridges — while directly behind it all loom the glass skyscrapers of the Shiodome business district. The juxtaposition of Edo-era serenity and 21st-century steel, framed in a single view, is one of the most photographed and most quietly moving sights in the city.
